notes.front: What is pilotage?
notes.back: Navigating by reference to visible landmarks.
notes.explanation: The handbook names it first of its three methods, beside dead reckoning and radio navigation.
notes.source: Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), ch. 16 “Navigation”, “Introduction”, PDF p. 1 (printed 16-1)
notes.evidence: chapter include pilotage—navigating by reference to visible landmarks, dead reckoning—computations of direction and distance from a known position, and radio navigation—by use of radio aids.
notes.example: Like driving with a paper road map and matching each town, river and railway you pass to the ones printed on it, but from the air.

notes.front: What is dead reckoning?
notes.back: Navigation by computing direction and distance from a known position.
notes.explanation: It relies on calculation rather than on seeing landmarks, which is what separates it from pilotage in the handbook’s list of methods.
notes.source: Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), ch. 16 “Navigation”, “Introduction”, PDF p. 1 (printed 16-1)
notes.evidence: landmarks, dead reckoning—computations of direction and distance from a known position, and radio navigation—by use of radio aids.
notes.example: Like a walker who knows her start point and pace and works out where she is after 20 minutes heading north, without looking at signposts.

notes.front: What is the true course (TC)?
notes.back: The course line measured on the chart, as a direction in degrees clockwise from true north.
notes.explanation: The handbook’s name for the measured chart course is the true course (TC); “true” means it is measured against a meridian, not the compass.
notes.source: Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), ch. 16 “Navigation”, “Measurement of Direction”, PDF p. 5 (printed 16-5)
notes.evidence: measured on the chart is known as the true course (TC).
notes.example: Like drawing a pencil line between two towns on a map and reading its angle against the map’s north–south grid lines.

notes.front: What is magnetic variation?
notes.back: The angle between true north and magnetic north, called east or west variation.
notes.explanation: It is east or west depending on whether magnetic north lies east or west of true north at that place.
notes.source: Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), ch. 16 “Navigation”, “Variation”, PDF p. 6 (printed 16-6)
notes.evidence: Variation is the angle between TN and magnetic north (MN). It is expressed as east variation or west variation depending upon whether MN is to the east or west of TN.
notes.example: Like a clock that runs a set number of minutes fast in one town and slow in another, so you correct it differently depending on where you are.

notes.front: What is compass deviation?
notes.back: Compass error caused by the aircraft’s own magnetic influences, which the pilot adds or subtracts.
notes.explanation: Unlike variation, which depends on location, deviation is peculiar to each aircraft and its onboard compass.
notes.source: Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), ch. 16 “Navigation”, “Magnetic Deviation”, PDF p. 7 (printed 16-7)
notes.evidence: Magnetic Deviation Because each aircraft has its own internal effect upon the onboard compass systems from its own localized magnetic
notes.example: Like a kitchen scale that always reads a little heavy because of the bowl sitting on it: the error comes from the set-up itself, not the place.

notes.front: What is the wind correction angle (WCA)?
notes.back: The angle, in degrees right or left of the TC, by which the aircraft is pointed into the wind to offset drift.
notes.explanation: If the wind is from the left the nose is pointed a set number of degrees left, and that angle is the WCA.
notes.source: Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), ch. 16 “Navigation”, “Effect of Wind”, PDF p. 9 (printed 16-9)
notes.evidence: correcting for wind drift. This is the wind correction angle (WCA) and is expressed in terms of degrees right or left of the TC.
notes.example: Like a swimmer crossing a river who aims a little upstream so the current carries her straight across.

notes.front: What is the true heading (TH)?
notes.back: The direction the aircraft’s nose points, in degrees clockwise from true north.
notes.explanation: It is where the nose points, not where the aircraft goes over the ground; with wind, the two usually differ.
notes.source: Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), ch. 16 “Navigation”, “Measurement of Direction”, PDF p. 6 (printed 16-6)
notes.evidence: The true heading (TH) is the direction in which the nose of
notes.example: Like the direction a rowing boat’s bow points while the current pushes it sideways.

notes.front: What is groundspeed (GS)?
notes.back: The aircraft’s speed of progress over the ground, which the wind changes but airspeed does not show.
notes.explanation: Moving air leaves airspeed unaffected, but it changes how fast the aircraft progresses over the ground.
notes.source: Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), ch. 16 “Navigation”, “Effect of Wind”, PDF p. 9 (printed 16-9)
notes.evidence: affected, but the progress of the aircraft over the ground is
notes.example: Like walking at your usual pace on an airport moving walkway: your walking speed is the same, but you pass the gates faster.

notes.front: What is a flight computer?
notes.back: A mechanical or electronic calculator that pilots use for flight-planning and navigation problems.
notes.explanation: It comes in two forms, mechanical and electronic.
notes.source: Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), ch. 16 “Navigation”, “Flight Computers”, PDF p. 12 (printed 16-12)
notes.evidence: computer called an E6B or electronic flight calculator. These
notes.example: Like a slide rule or a calculator app, but with scales laid out for time, speed, distance, fuel and wind.

notes.front: What is a visual checkpoint?
notes.back: A prominent feature on the route, chosen before flight, that the pilot uses to confirm position.
notes.explanation: Pilotage is navigation by reference to such checkpoints, so they are chosen to stand out in the area flown over.
notes.source: Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), ch. 16 “Navigation”, “Pilotage”, PDF p. 12 (printed 16-12)
notes.evidence: The checkpoints selected should be prominent features
notes.example: Like the distinctive church spire a hiker plans to pass at the halfway mark to confirm she is on the right trail.

notes.front: What is a terminal area chart (TAC)?
notes.back: A VFR chart for flying in or near Class B airspace, drawn at a scale of 1:250,000.
notes.explanation: At 1:250,000 an inch covers about 3.43 NM, half the ground an inch covers on a sectional chart.
notes.source: Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), ch. 16 “Navigation”, “VFR Terminal Area Charts”, PDF p. 2 (printed 16-2)
notes.evidence: Class B airspace. They have a scale of 1:250,000 (1 inch
notes.example: Like a city street map that zooms in on the centre, where the regional road map would be too cramped to read.

notes.front: What is a VHF omnidirectional range (VOR)?
notes.back: A ground radio navigation aid operating between 108.0 and 117.95 MHz.
notes.explanation: Its signals are limited by line of sight, so its range grows with the altitude of the receiving aircraft.
notes.source: Aeronautical Information Manual, para. 1-1-3 “VHF Omni-directional Range (VOR)”
notes.evidence: VORs operate within the 108.0 to 117.95 MHz frequency band and have a power output necessary to provide coverage within their assigned operational service volume. They are subject to line-of-sight restrictions, and the range varies proportionally to the altitude of the receiving equipment.
notes.example: Like a lighthouse, but one sending a radio signal that tells a receiver which direction it lies from the station.

notes.front: What is a radial?
notes.back: A line of magnetic bearing extending outward from a VOR station.
notes.explanation: Radials point away from the station and are referenced to magnetic, not true, north.
notes.source: Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), ch. 16 “Navigation”, “Very High Frequency (VHF) Omnidirectional Range (VOR)”, PDF p. 22 (printed 16-22)
notes.evidence: Therefore, a radial is defined as a line of magnetic
notes.example: Like the spokes of a bicycle wheel, each numbered by its direction out from the hub.

notes.front: What is a course deviation indicator (CDI)?
notes.back: The VOR display found in most training aircraft, whose needle shows left or right displacement from the selected course.
notes.explanation: The handbook describes it as the usual VOR instrument in training aircraft.
notes.source: Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), ch. 16 “Navigation”, “Course Deviation Indicator (CDI)”, PDF p. 23 (printed 16-23)
notes.evidence: The CDI is found in most training aircraft. It consists of an omnibearing selector (OBS) sometimes referred to as the
notes.example: Like a lane-keeping display in a car that shows how far you have drifted from the centre of the lane.

notes.front: What is the omnibearing selector (OBS)?
notes.back: The rotatable course selector on the CDI, used to select a radial or find the radial the aircraft is on.
notes.explanation: It is part of the CDI, and is sometimes simply called the course selector.
notes.source: Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), ch. 16 “Navigation”, “Course Deviation Indicator (CDI)”, PDF p. 23 (printed 16-23)
notes.evidence: The course selector is an azimuth dial that can be rotated to select a desired radial or to determine the radial over which
notes.example: Like the dial on a combination lock: you turn it to the number (here, the course) you want.

notes.front: What does the TO/FROM indicator show?
notes.back: Whether the course set on the course selector leads to the station or away from it.
notes.explanation: With a “TO” the set course, flown, takes the aircraft to the station; with “FROM”, away from it.
notes.source: Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), ch. 16 “Navigation”, “Course Deviation Indicator (CDI)”, PDF p. 24 (printed 16-24)
notes.evidence: If the flag displays a “TO,” the course shown on the course selector must be flown to the station.
notes.example: Like a sign on a motorway gantry saying whether the road ahead heads towards the city or away from it.

notes.front: What is distance measuring equipment (DME)?
notes.back: Airborne and ground equipment that times a radio signal’s round trip to give distance, in nautical miles, to the station.
notes.explanation: It measures time, not distance directly: the airborne unit converts the signal’s round-trip time into nautical miles.
notes.source: Aeronautical Information Manual, para. 1-1-7 “Distance Measuring Equipment (DME)”
notes.evidence: The time required for the round trip of this signal exchange is measured in the airborne DME unit and is translated into distance (nautical miles) from the aircraft to the ground station.
notes.example: Like shouting at a cliff and timing the echo to work out how far away it is.

notes.front: What is an automatic direction finder (ADF)?
notes.back: An aircraft receiver whose needle points to the tuned ground station, a nondirectional radio beacon.
notes.explanation: To navigate with it, the pilot tunes the ground station and reads where the needle points.
notes.source: Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), ch. 16 “Navigation”, “Automatic Direction Finder (ADF)”, PDF p. 29 (printed 16-29)
notes.evidence: dial and points to the station to which the receiver is tuned.
notes.example: Like a compass needle that points at a radio mast instead of at magnetic north.

notes.front: What is the wide area augmentation system (WAAS)?
notes.back: An FAA system that improves the accuracy, integrity and availability of GPS signals.
notes.explanation: The aim, once it is complete, is for GPS to be usable from takeoff through approach.
notes.source: Aeronautical Information Manual, para. 1-1-18 “Wide Area Augmentation System (WAAS)”
notes.evidence: The FAA developed the WAAS to improve the accuracy, integrity and availability of GPS signals. WAAS will allow GPS to be used, as the aviation navigation system, from takeoff through approach when it is complete.
notes.example: Like a proofreader who checks a report as it is written and sends corrections to every reader.

notes.front: What is receiver autonomous integrity monitoring (RAIM)?
notes.back: A GPS receiver’s ability to check its own integrity by making sure the available satellite signals meet the needs of that phase of flight.
notes.explanation: The Aeronautical Information Manual says that without it the pilot has no assurance that the GPS position is sound.
notes.source: Aeronautical Information Manual, para. 1-1-17 “Global Positioning System (GPS)”
notes.evidence: RAIM is the capability of a GPS receiver to perform integrity monitoring on itself by ensuring available satellite signals meet the integrity requirements for a given phase of flight. Without RAIM, the pilot has no assurance of the GPS position integrity.
notes.example: Like a sat-nav that cross-checks one extra satellite and warns you when the fix may be wrong.

notes.front: What is an electronic flight bag (EFB)?
notes.back: A portable electronic device used to display charts and data in flight.
notes.explanation: An applicant who trained with one may use it on the practical test but must show the knowledge, risk management and skill it calls for.
notes.source: Private Pilot for Airplane Category ACS (FAA-S-ACS-6C), Airman Certification Standards, Appendix: use of an electronic flight bag, PDF p. 85
notes.evidence: trained using a portable electronic flight bag (EFB) to display charts and data and wishes to use the EFB during the practical test, the applicant is expected to demonstrate appropriate knowledge, risk management, and skill appropriate to its use.
notes.example: Like carrying a tablet with the charts and airport guides loaded instead of a bag full of paper.

notes.front: What does activating a VFR flight plan give the pilot?
notes.back: VFR search and rescue services.
notes.explanation: A filed plan records the route and timing; activating it is what brings the search and rescue cover.
notes.source: Aeronautical Information Manual, para. 5-1-5 “Flight Plan - VFR Flights”
notes.evidence: Activating the flight plan will ensure that you receive VFR Search and Rescue services.
notes.example: Like telling a friend your hiking route and return time, so someone knows where to look if you do not come back.

notes.front: What is VFR flight following?
notes.back: Radar flight following or advisories that a radar facility gives a VFR aircraft en route.
notes.explanation: The facility treats losing radar and radio contact, without the service being ended, as a possible emergency.
notes.source: Aeronautical Information Manual, para. 6-2-6 “Search and Rescue”
notes.evidence: Radar facilities providing radar flight following or advisories consider the loss of radar and radios, without service termination notice, to be a possible emergency.
notes.example: Like a lifeguard who watches your swim from the tower and calls out hazards, but who notices at once if you vanish.

notes.front: A sectional chart has a scale of {{c1::1:500,000}}, so 1 inch is about 6.86 NM or 8 SM.
notes.explanation: Knowing the scale lets a pilot turn distances measured on the chart into distances over the ground.
notes.source: Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), ch. 16 “Navigation”, “Sectional Charts”, PDF p. 2 (printed 16-2)
notes.evidence: today. The charts have a scale of 1:500,000 (1 inch = 6.86 nautical miles (NM) or approximately 8 statute miles (SM)),

notes.front: On a sectional chart, a water tower you pass lies half an inch to one side of your course line. Roughly how far off course is it on the ground?
notes.back: About 4 SM (3.43 NM).
notes.explanation: At 1 inch = 8 SM or 6.86 NM, half an inch is half those distances.
notes.source: Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), ch. 16 “Navigation”, “Pilotage”, PDF p. 12 (printed 16-12)
notes.evidence: remember that the scale of a sectional chart is 1 inch = 8 SM or 6.86 NM.
notes.choices:
A) About 4 SM
B) About 8 SM
C) About 1 SM
notes.choicesExplained: B: 8 SM is a full inch on a sectional. C: far too small; half an inch is about 4 SM.

notes.front: On this sectional obstacle label, which number is the obstacle’s height above ground?
notes.back: 849, the number in parentheses; 1349 is the elevation of its top above MSL.
notes.explanation: The Chart Users’ Guide prints the height above ground in parentheses beneath the elevation above sea level.
notes.source: FAA Aeronautical Chart Users' Guide (9 July 2026), “Obstacles”, PDF p. 11
notes.evidence: The AGL height is in parentheses below the MSL elevation.

notes.front: On a sectional chart, an airport symbol and its data are printed in magenta. What does the colour tell you?
notes.back: The airport has no control tower; towered airports are shown in blue.
notes.explanation: The chart uses blue for airports with control towers and magenta for all others.
notes.source: FAA Aeronautical Chart Users' Guide (9 July 2026), “Airports”, PDF p. 15
notes.evidence: Airports with Control Towers (CT) and their related data are shown in blue. All other airports and their related data are shown in magenta.
notes.choices:
A) No control tower
B) A control tower operates
C) The airport is military
notes.choicesExplained: B: towered airports are blue, not magenta. C: the colour marks towered or not; it says nothing about military use.

notes.front: Your true course out to a lake is 030°. What true course brings you straight back?
notes.back: 210°, the reciprocal.
notes.explanation: The return trip is called the reciprocal and differs from the outbound course by 180°.
notes.source: Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), ch. 16 “Navigation”, “Measurement of Direction”, PDF p. 5 (printed 16-5)
notes.evidence: a TC of 065°, whereas the return trip (called the reciprocal)
notes.choicesExplained: B: 330° is 030° mirrored about north, not the reverse direction. C: flying 030° again takes you further away.

notes.front: After finding the TH, in what order are corrections applied to reach compass heading?
notes.back: TH ± variation = magnetic heading; magnetic heading ± deviation = compass heading.
notes.explanation: Variation converts from true to magnetic, and deviation then converts from magnetic to what this aircraft’s compass shows.
notes.source: Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), ch. 16 “Navigation”, “Effect of Wind”, PDF p. 9 (printed 16-9)
notes.evidence: correction applied resulting in a TH, the sequence TH ± variation (V) = magnetic heading (MH) ± deviation (D) = compass heading (CH) is followed to arrive at compass heading.

notes.front: TC 120°, wind from the right needing 5° correction, variation 7°W, deviation −2°. What compass heading do you fly?
notes.back: 130°: TH 125°, magnetic heading 132°, compass heading 130°.
notes.explanation: Add the WCA for a wind from the right, add west variation, then apply the deviation.
notes.source: Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), ch. 16 “Navigation”, “Effect of Wind”, PDF p. 9 (printed 16-9)
notes.evidence: correction applied resulting in a TH, the sequence TH ± variation (V) = magnetic heading (MH) ± deviation (D) = compass heading (CH) is followed to arrive at compass heading.
notes.choicesExplained: B: subtracts the 7° west variation instead of adding it (125 − 7 − 2 = 116). C: ignores wind, variation and deviation.

notes.front: On a chart, what is the agonic line?
notes.back: The line joining points where there is no variation between true and magnetic north.
notes.explanation: Isogonic lines join points of equal variation; the agonic line is the one where that variation is zero.
notes.source: Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), ch. 16 “Navigation”, “Variation”, PDF p. 6 (printed 16-6)
notes.evidence: magenta lines called isogonic lines that connect points of equal magnetic variation. (The line connecting points at which there is no variation between TN and MN is the agonic

notes.front: To remember how to apply variation: “east is least ({{c1::subtract}}) and west is best (add).”
notes.explanation: The memory phrase covers converting a true direction to a magnetic one.
notes.source: Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), ch. 16 “Navigation”, “Variation”, PDF p. 8 (printed 16-8)
notes.evidence: is the phrase “east is least (subtract) and west is best (add).”

notes.front: Your true heading is 250° and the isogonic line nearby shows 9°E. What is your magnetic heading?
notes.explanation: East variation is subtracted: “east is least”.
notes.source: Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), ch. 16 “Navigation”, “Variation”, PDF p. 8 (printed 16-8)
notes.evidence: Remember, if variation is west, add; if east, subtract. One
notes.choicesExplained: B: adds east variation; west is added, east subtracted. C: ignores variation.

notes.front: What are three sources inside an aircraft that can deflect its compass?
notes.back: Among others: electrical circuits, radios and the engine.
notes.explanation: The handbook’s list also includes lights and tools; their pull on the needle is the deviation.
notes.source: Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), ch. 16 “Navigation”, “Deviation”, PDF p. 8 (printed 16-8)
notes.evidence: aircraft, such as electrical circuits, radio, lights, tools, engine,

notes.front: Is compass deviation the same on every heading and in every aircraft?
notes.back: No: it differs between aircraft and may vary with heading in the same aircraft.
notes.explanation: So a correction found for one heading, or one aircraft, cannot simply be reused for another.
notes.source: Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), ch. 16 “Navigation”, “Deviation”, PDF p. 8 (printed 16-8)
notes.evidence: deviation. The deviation is different for each aircraft, and it also may vary for different headings in the same aircraft.

notes.front: Your deviation card reads “For 120, Steer 117”. You want to fly a magnetic heading of 120°. What do you steer by the compass?
notes.explanation: The card gives, for each magnetic heading, the compass heading to steer.
notes.source: Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), ch. 16 “Navigation”, “Deviation”, PDF p. 8 (printed 16-8)
notes.evidence: the compass showing the addition or subtraction required to
notes.choicesExplained: B: applies the correction the wrong way. C: ignores the card.

notes.front: What is the difference between magnetic variation and compass deviation?
notes.back: Variation depends on where you are (true vs magnetic north); deviation depends on the aircraft and heading.
notes.explanation: Variation comes from the earth’s magnetism at a location; deviation from magnetic influences inside the aircraft.
notes.source: Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), ch. 16 “Navigation”, “Deviation”, PDF p. 8 (printed 16-8)
notes.evidence: deviation. The deviation is different for each aircraft, and it also may vary for different headings in the same aircraft.

notes.front: When the wind blows from the right of the TC, the WCA is {{c1::added}} to find the TH.
notes.explanation: Pointing into a wind from the right means turning right, to a larger number.
notes.source: Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), ch. 16 “Navigation”, “Wind Triangle or Vector Analysis”, PDF p. 15 (printed 16-15)
notes.evidence: blows from the right of TC, the angle is added; if from

notes.front: TC 180°. The wind triangle gives a WCA of 8° with the wind from the right. What is the TH?
notes.explanation: A wind from the right adds the WCA to the TC.
notes.source: Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), ch. 16 “Navigation”, “Wind Triangle or Vector Analysis”, PDF p. 15 (printed 16-15)
notes.evidence: blows from the right of TC, the angle is added; if from
notes.choicesExplained: B: subtracts the WCA, which is right only for a wind from the left. C: ignores the wind.

notes.front: You cruise at 110 knots airspeed with a 15-knot wind directly behind you. What is your groundspeed?
notes.back: 125 knots.
notes.explanation: A direct tailwind adds its full speed to the airspeed over the ground.
notes.source: Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), ch. 16 “Navigation”, “Effect of Wind”, PDF p. 9 (printed 16-9)
notes.evidence: 120 plus 20 or a GS of 140 knots. On the other hand, if the
notes.choices:
A) 125 knots
B) 95 knots
C) 110 knots
notes.choicesExplained: B: subtracts the wind, which applies to a headwind. C: ignores the wind’s effect over the ground.

notes.front: The wind triangle, the pilot’s version of vector analysis, is {{c1::the basis of dead reckoning}}.
notes.explanation: Dead reckoning’s heading and groundspeed come from solving it.
notes.source: Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), ch. 16 “Navigation”, “Wind Triangle or Vector Analysis”, PDF p. 13 (printed 16-13)
notes.evidence: of vector analysis, is the basis of dead reckoning.

notes.front: Over featureless sea, a pilot holds a calculated heading and times the leg from a known departure point. Which method is this?
notes.back: Dead reckoning.
notes.explanation: Computing direction and distance from a known position, with no landmarks, is dead reckoning.
notes.source: Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), ch. 16 “Navigation”, “Introduction”, PDF p. 1 (printed 16-1)
notes.evidence: landmarks, dead reckoning—computations of direction and distance from a known position, and radio navigation—by use of radio aids.
notes.choices:
A) Dead reckoning
B) Pilotage
C) Radio navigation
notes.choicesExplained: B: pilotage needs visible landmarks, which the sea lacks. C: no radio aid is being used.

notes.front: A pilot follows a river until a dam, then turns to follow a railway to the destination. Which method is this?
notes.back: Pilotage.
notes.explanation: Navigating by visible landmarks such as rivers, dams and railways is pilotage.
notes.source: Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), ch. 16 “Navigation”, “Introduction”, PDF p. 1 (printed 16-1)
notes.evidence: chapter include pilotage—navigating by reference to visible landmarks, dead reckoning—computations of direction and distance from a known position, and radio navigation—by use of radio aids.
notes.choices:
A) Pilotage
B) Dead reckoning
C) Radio navigation
notes.choicesExplained: B: no computation of heading and time is being relied on. C: no radio aid is being used.

notes.front: Which VFR waypoints may be used in radio calls to ATC?
notes.back: Those collocated with a visual checkpoint and named after it; stand-alone five-letter waypoint names are not for ATC communications.
notes.explanation: A collocated waypoint takes the checkpoint’s pronounceable name, marked by a small magenta flag on the chart.
notes.source: Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), ch. 16 “Navigation”, “VFR Waypoints”, PDF p. 33 (printed 16-33)
notes.evidence: visual checkpoint and may be used for ATC communications.

notes.front: Time in flight = distance ÷ {{c1::groundspeed}}.
notes.explanation: Groundspeed, not airspeed, is the rate at which the distance over the ground is covered.
notes.source: Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), ch. 16 “Navigation”, “Time T = D/GS”, PDF p. 11 (printed 16-11)

notes.back: 1 hour 30 minutes.
notes.explanation: 150 ÷ 100 = 1.5 hours, and 0.5 hour × 60 = 30 minutes.
notes.source: Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), ch. 16 “Navigation”, “Time T = D/GS”, PDF p. 11 (printed 16-11)
notes.evidence: To find the time (T) in flight, divide the distance (D) by the
notes.choices:
A) 1 hour 30 minutes
B) 1 hour 50 minutes
C) 1 hour 5 minutes
notes.choicesExplained: B: reads 1.5 hours as 1 hour 50 minutes; 0.5 hour is 30 minutes. C: 1.5 hours is not 1 hour 5 minutes.

notes.front: Two checkpoints 24 NM apart are passed 12 minutes apart. What is your groundspeed?
notes.back: 120 knots.
notes.explanation: GS = distance ÷ time: 24 NM ÷ 0.2 hour = 120 knots.
notes.source: Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), ch. 16 “Navigation”, “GS = D/T”, PDF p. 11 (printed 16-11)
notes.evidence: To find the GS, divide the distance flown by the time
notes.choices:
A) 120 knots
B) 200 knots
C) 2 knots
notes.choicesExplained: B: divides by 0.12 instead of 0.2 hour. C: divides by 12 without converting minutes to hours.

notes.front: How is the fuel needed for a flight calculated?
notes.back: Estimated flight time multiplied by the rate of fuel consumption.
notes.explanation: Fuel burn is quoted per hour, so the time en route sets the total.
notes.source: Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), ch. 16 “Navigation”, “Fuel Consumption”, PDF p. 12 (printed 16-12)

notes.front: A leg will take 2 hours 30 minutes and the airplane burns 9 gallons per hour. How much fuel will the leg use?
notes.back: 22.5 gallons.
notes.explanation: Fuel = time × rate: 2.5 × 9 = 22.5, before any reserve is added.
notes.source: Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), ch. 16 “Navigation”, “Fuel Consumption”, PDF p. 12 (printed 16-12)

notes.choices:
A) 22.5 gallons
B) 20.7 gallons
C) 27 gallons
notes.choicesExplained: B: treats 2:30 as 2.3 hours. C: uses 3 hours.

notes.front: With wind present, which speed must be used to calculate fuel consumption?
notes.back: Groundspeed.
notes.explanation: Groundspeed sets how long the flight takes, and fuel used is that time multiplied by the burn rate.
notes.source: Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), ch. 16 “Navigation”, “Fuel Consumption”, PDF p. 12 (printed 16-12)

notes.front: For a VFR flight by day, an airplane must carry enough fuel to reach the first point of intended landing and then fly at normal cruising speed for at least {{c1::30 minutes}}.
notes.explanation: The requirement applies before the flight begins and takes account of wind and forecast weather.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 91.151 Fuel requirements for flight in VFR conditions (eCFR), (a)(1)
notes.evidence: No person may begin a flight in an airplane under VFR conditions unless (considering wind and forecast weather conditions) there is enough fuel to fly to the first point of intended landing and, assuming normal cruising speed— (1) During the day, to fly after that for at least 30 minutes; or
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · FAA-S-ACS-6C and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: For a VFR flight at night, an airplane must carry enough fuel to reach the first point of intended landing and then fly at normal cruising speed for at least {{c1::45 minutes}}.
notes.explanation: The night reserve is 15 minutes longer than the day reserve.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 91.151 Fuel requirements for flight in VFR conditions (eCFR), (a)(2)
notes.evidence: (2) At night, to fly after that for at least 45 minutes.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · FAA-S-ACS-6C and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: A night VFR flight to the first landing airport is planned at 1 hour 40 minutes, including wind. What is the least flying time the fuel on board must allow?
notes.back: 2 hours 25 minutes.
notes.explanation: The night reserve adds 45 minutes at normal cruising speed to the time to the first point of intended landing.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 91.151 Fuel requirements for flight in VFR conditions (eCFR), (a)(2)
notes.evidence: (2) At night, to fly after that for at least 45 minutes.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · FAA-S-ACS-6C and 14 CFR as in force
notes.choices:
A) 2 hours 25 minutes
B) 2 hours 10 minutes
C) 1 hour 55 minutes
notes.choicesExplained: B: uses the 30-minute day reserve. C: adds only 15 minutes.

notes.front: A daytime VFR flight to the destination (the first landing) takes 1 hour 10 minutes with the forecast wind. What is the least flying time the fuel must allow?
notes.back: 1 hour 40 minutes.
notes.explanation: By day the regulation adds a 30-minute reserve at normal cruising speed.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 91.151 Fuel requirements for flight in VFR conditions (eCFR), (a)(1)
notes.evidence: (1) During the day, to fly after that for at least 30 minutes; or
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · FAA-S-ACS-6C and 14 CFR as in force
notes.choices:
A) 1 hour 40 minutes
B) 1 hour 55 minutes
C) 1 hour 10 minutes
notes.choicesExplained: B: uses the 45-minute night reserve. C: leaves no reserve at all.

notes.front: How do the VFR fuel reserves for an airplane differ by day and at night?
notes.back: Day: 30 minutes; night: 45 minutes, both at normal cruising speed after the first point of intended landing.
notes.explanation: Both are minimums in the same rule; the night figure is the larger.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 91.151 Fuel requirements for flight in VFR conditions (eCFR), (a)(2)
notes.evidence: (2) At night, to fly after that for at least 45 minutes.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · FAA-S-ACS-6C and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: You expect to land at 1545 Central Standard Time. What arrival time do you give in UTC?
notes.explanation: Central Standard Time converts to UTC by adding 6 hours.
notes.source: Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), ch. 16 “Navigation”, “Time Zones”, PDF p. 5 (printed 16-5)

notes.explanation: Pacific Standard Time adds 8 hours; for Daylight Saving Time, 1 hour is subtracted from that result.
notes.source: Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), ch. 16 “Navigation”, “Time Zones”, PDF p. 5 (printed 16-5)

notes.choices:
A) 1600 UTC
B) 1700 UTC

notes.front: Is a VFR flight plan normally required within the continental United States?
notes.back: No, not normally.
notes.explanation: Exceptions exist: VFR flights into an air defense identification zone must file a defense VFR flight plan.
notes.source: Aeronautical Information Manual, para. 5-1-5 “Flight Plan - VFR Flights”
notes.evidence: Within the continental U.S., a VFR flight plan is not normally required. VFR flights (except for DoD and law enforcement flights) into an Air Defense Identification Zone (ADIZ) are required to file DVFR flight plans.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · FAA-S-ACS-6C and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: Who activates a VFR flight plan?
notes.back: The pilot, with a Flight Service Station; control towers do not activate it automatically.
notes.explanation: Filing alone does not start the plan, and a tower will not start it for you.
notes.source: Aeronautical Information Manual, para. 5-1-5 “Flight Plan - VFR Flights”
notes.evidence: Pilots are responsible for activating flight plans with a Flight Service Station. Control tower personnel do not automatically activate VFR flight plans.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · FAA-S-ACS-6C and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: You filed with an assumed departure time of 1400 but leave at 1440 without updating it. What happens if you go missing?
notes.back: Search and rescue will be based on the 1400 assumed departure time.
notes.explanation: The plan becomes active at the assumed time; revising the departure time or estimated arrival time is the pilot’s job.
notes.source: Aeronautical Information Manual, para. 5-1-5 “Flight Plan - VFR Flights”
notes.evidence: If not updated, search and rescue activities will be based on the assumed departure time.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · FAA-S-ACS-6C and 14 CFR as in force
notes.choices:
A) Search begins from the 1400 assumed time
B) Flight Service notices the real departure
C) The plan is cancelled automatically
notes.choicesExplained: B: the assumed time activates the plan without anyone watching the departure. C: nothing cancels it; it stays active on the assumed time.

notes.front: If a VFR flight plan is not closed, when do search and rescue procedures start?
notes.back: If you fail to report or cancel within half an hour after your estimated time of arrival.
notes.explanation: Half an hour after the estimated arrival time is the trigger, so a forgotten close can launch a search.
notes.source: Aeronautical Information Manual, para. 5-1-14 “Closing VFR/DVFR Flight Plans”
notes.evidence: If you fail to report or cancel your flight plan within 1/2 hour after your ETA, search and rescue procedures are started.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · FAA-S-ACS-6C and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: You land at a towered airport while on a VFR flight plan. The tower clears you to taxi to parking. Is your flight plan closed?
notes.back: No. Towers do not automatically close VFR flight plans; you must close it with Flight Service.
notes.explanation: Towers do not know whether a particular VFR aircraft is on a flight plan.
notes.source: Aeronautical Information Manual, para. 5-1-14 “Closing VFR/DVFR Flight Plans”
notes.evidence: Control towers do not automatically close VFR or DVFR flight plans since they do not know if a particular VFR aircraft is on a flight plan.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · FAA-S-ACS-6C and 14 CFR as in force
notes.choices:
A) No, the pilot must close it
B) Yes, landing closes it
C) Yes, the tower closes it for you
notes.choicesExplained: B: landing does not close a plan. C: towers do not automatically close VFR flight plans.

notes.front: Which details of the aircraft must a VFR flight plan include?
notes.back: Its identification number (and radio call sign if necessary) and its type.
notes.explanation: The radio call sign is added only if necessary.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 91.153 VFR flight plan: Information required (eCFR), (a)(1)
notes.evidence: (1) The aircraft identification number and, if necessary, its radio call sign. (2) The type of the aircraft
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · FAA-S-ACS-6C and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: Whose name and address must a VFR flight plan give?
notes.back: The pilot in command’s full name and address.
notes.explanation: For a formation flight it is the formation commander’s instead.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 91.153 VFR flight plan: Information required (eCFR), (a)(3)
notes.evidence: (3) The full name and address of the pilot in command or, in the case of a formation flight, the formation commander.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · FAA-S-ACS-6C and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: What must a VFR flight plan say about the departure?
notes.back: The point and proposed time of departure.
notes.explanation: At filing, the rule asks for a proposed time, not the actual one.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 91.153 VFR flight plan: Information required (eCFR), (a)(4)
notes.evidence: (4) The point and proposed time of departure.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · FAA-S-ACS-6C and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: Which speed is given in a VFR flight plan with the proposed route and cruising altitude?
notes.back: True airspeed at that altitude.
notes.explanation: The rule groups route, cruising altitude (or flight level) and true airspeed in one item.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 91.153 VFR flight plan: Information required (eCFR), (a)(5)
notes.evidence: (5) The proposed route, cruising altitude (or flight level), and true airspeed at that altitude.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · FAA-S-ACS-6C and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: What arrival details must a VFR flight plan give?
notes.back: The point of first intended landing and the estimated elapsed time until over it.
notes.explanation: It is the first landing, not the final destination of a multi-stop trip, that the rule names.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 91.153 VFR flight plan: Information required (eCFR), (a)(6)
notes.evidence: (6) The point of first intended landing and the estimated elapsed time until over that point.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · FAA-S-ACS-6C and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: A VFR flight plan states the amount of fuel on board in {{c1::hours}}.
notes.explanation: Gallons are turned into hours by dividing by the expected fuel burn.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 91.153 VFR flight plan: Information required (eCFR), (a)(7)
notes.evidence: (7) The amount of fuel on board (in hours).
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · FAA-S-ACS-6C and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: Which count of people must a VFR flight plan include?
notes.back: The number of persons in the aircraft, unless that is otherwise readily available to the FAA.
notes.explanation: The rule lets this item be left out when the FAA already has it.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 91.153 VFR flight plan: Information required (eCFR), (a)(8)
notes.evidence: (8) The number of persons in the aircraft, except where that information is otherwise readily available to the FAA.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · FAA-S-ACS-6C and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: You have 40 gallons of usable fuel and burn 8 gallons per hour. What do you enter as fuel on board in the flight plan?
notes.back: 5 hours 00 minutes.
notes.explanation: Fuel on board is entered in hours and minutes: usable fuel divided by the rate of consumption.
notes.source: Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), ch. 16 “Navigation”, “Filing a VFR Flight Plan”, PDF p. 22 (printed 16-22)
notes.evidence: Item 12 is the fuel on board in hours and minutes. This
notes.choices:
A) 5 hours 00 minutes
B) 40 gallons
C) 4 hours 30 minutes
notes.choicesExplained: B: the entry is in time, not gallons. C: 40 ÷ 8 is 5, not 4.5.

notes.front: What is the only positive way to identify a VOR?
notes.back: Its Morse code identification, or its recorded voice identification ending in the word “VOR”.
notes.explanation: Anything else heard on the frequency, such as a person’s voice, is not a positive identification.
notes.source: Aeronautical Information Manual, para. 1-1-3 “VHF Omni-directional Range (VOR)”
notes.evidence: The only positive method of identifying a VOR is by its Morse Code identification or by the recorded automatic voice identification which is always indicated by use of the word “VOR” following the range's name.

notes.front: You tune a VOR and hear T-E-S-T in Morse code instead of its identifier. What does this suggest?
notes.back: It may be undergoing maintenance; do not rely on it for navigation.
notes.explanation: During maintenance a VOR may radiate a T-E-S-T code or have its identification removed.
notes.source: Aeronautical Information Manual, para. 1-1-3 “VHF Omni-directional Range (VOR)”
notes.evidence: During periods of maintenance, the facility may radiate a T-E-S-T code (- ● ●●● -) or the code may be removed.
notes.choices:
A) Possible maintenance: do not rely on it
B) It is working normally
C) It is a VOR test facility for receiver checks
notes.choicesExplained: B: a normal VOR sends its own identifier. C: a VOR test facility is identified by dots or a continuous tone, not T-E-S-T.

notes.front: How are VOR radials numbered?
notes.back: From 001, which is 1° east of magnetic north, around to 360.
notes.explanation: Radials are referenced to magnetic north, so their numbers are magnetic directions.
notes.source: Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), ch. 16 “Navigation”, “Very High Frequency (VHF) Omnidirectional Range (VOR)”, PDF p. 22 (printed 16-22)
notes.evidence: identified by numbers beginning with 001, which is 1° east

notes.front: You are due east of a VOR. Which radial are you on?
notes.back: The 090 radial.
notes.explanation: A radial is a magnetic bearing outward from the station, so due east of it is 090.
notes.source: Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), ch. 16 “Navigation”, “Very High Frequency (VHF) Omnidirectional Range (VOR)”, PDF p. 22 (printed 16-22)
notes.evidence: Therefore, a radial is defined as a line of magnetic
notes.choicesExplained: B: 270 is the radial due west; it would be your course to the station. C: 360 is due north.

notes.front: What does the CDI needle do when the aircraft drifts off the selected radial?
notes.back: It moves to the right or left of centre.
notes.explanation: The needle shows where the selected radial lies relative to the aircraft.
notes.source: Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), ch. 16 “Navigation”, “Course Deviation Indicator (CDI)”, PDF p. 24 (printed 16-24)
notes.evidence: to the right or left if the aircraft is flown or drifting away from the radial which is set in the course selector.

notes.front: You turn the OBS until the needle centres with a FROM flag, reading 135. Where are you relative to the station?
notes.back: On the 135 radial, southeast of the station.
notes.explanation: With the needle centred and FROM showing, the course selector reads the radial the aircraft is on.
notes.source: Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), ch. 16 “Navigation”, “Course Deviation Indicator (CDI)”, PDF p. 24 (printed 16-24)
notes.evidence: needle is centered, the radial (magnetic course “FROM” the
notes.choices:
A) On the 135 radial, southeast of it
B) On the 315 radial, northwest of it
C) Heading 135 towards it
notes.choicesExplained: B: that would give TO with 135 set. C: the OBS shows position, not the aircraft’s heading.

notes.front: Your needle centres with 060 set and a TO flag. Which radial are you on?
notes.back: The 240 radial; flying 060 takes you to the station.
notes.explanation: With TO showing, the set course is the magnetic course to the station, the reciprocal of your radial.
notes.source: Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), ch. 16 “Navigation”, “Course Deviation Indicator (CDI)”, PDF p. 24 (printed 16-24)
notes.evidence: station) or its reciprocal (magnetic course “TO” the station)
notes.choicesExplained: B: 060 would be your radial only with a FROM flag. C: 150 is 90° off the set course; your radial is the reciprocal, 060 + 180 = 240.

notes.front: When flying to a VOR, always fly the selected course with a “{{c1::TO}}” indication.
notes.explanation: Flying away from a station, the matching rule is to fly the selected course with a “FROM” indication.
notes.source: Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), ch. 16 “Navigation”, “Tracking With VOR”, PDF p. 26 (printed 16-26)
notes.evidence: course with a “TO” indication. When flying “FROM” a station, always fly the selected course with a “FROM”

notes.front: What happens to the CDI needle if you fly toward a VOR with a FROM indication showing?
notes.back: Its action is reversed: it deflects opposite to the way it should.
notes.explanation: This is why the selected course should match the direction of flight, TO when inbound.
notes.source: Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), ch. 16 “Navigation”, “Tracking With VOR”, PDF p. 26 (printed 16-26)
notes.evidence: with a “TO” indication, the course deviation needle indicates in a direction opposite to that which it should

notes.front: At a VOR test facility, your CDI centres with the OBS at 180. Which flag should show if the receiver is accurate?
notes.back: TO.
notes.explanation: On a test signal the OBS should read 0 with FROM, or 180 with TO, when the needle is centred.
notes.source: Aeronautical Information Manual, para. 1-1-4 “VOR Receiver Check”
notes.evidence: the omni-bearing selector should read 0 degrees with the to/from indication showing “from” or the omni-bearing selector should read 180 degrees with the to/from indication showing “to.”
notes.choices:
A) TO
B) FROM
C) Either flag
notes.choicesExplained: B: FROM is correct only with the OBS at 0. C: only one flag is correct for each setting.

notes.front: What errors fail a VOR ground check and an airborne check, before flight under IFR?
notes.back: More than ±4° on a ground check or ±6° on an airborne check.
notes.explanation: IFR flight must not be attempted until the source of such an error is corrected.
notes.source: Aeronautical Information Manual, para. 1-1-4 “VOR Receiver Check”
notes.evidence: Should an error in excess of plus or minus 4 degrees be indicated through use of a ground check, or plus or minus 6 degrees using the airborne check, Instrument Flight Rules (IFR) flight must not be attempted without first correcting the source of the error.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · FAA-S-ACS-6C and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: Are VOR accuracy checks required for VFR flight?
notes.back: No, but the handbook suggests using the IFR tolerances as a guide.
notes.explanation: The handbook offers the IFR tolerances only as a guide to acceptable accuracy.
notes.source: Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), ch. 16 “Navigation”, “VOR Operational Checks”, PDF p. 23 (printed 16-23)
notes.evidence: radials the station transmits. There are not specific tolerances in VOR checks required for VFR flight. But as a guide to

notes.front: Into which three classes were VOR standard service volumes originally divided?
notes.back: Terminal (T), Low (L) and High (H).
notes.explanation: The letters T, L and H name the three classes of navigation aid.
notes.source: Aeronautical Information Manual, para. 1-1-8 “NAVAID Service Volumes”
notes.evidence: The three original SSVs are shown in FIG 1-1-1 and are designated with three classes of NAVAIDs: Terminal (T), Low (L), and High (H).

notes.front: Is DME distance the horizontal distance to the station?
notes.back: No: it is slant range distance, the direct distance, so it is affected by altitude.
notes.explanation: So the reading includes the aircraft’s height as well as its distance along the ground.
notes.source: Aeronautical Information Manual, para. 1-1-7 “Distance Measuring Equipment (DME)”
notes.evidence: Distance information received from DME equipment is SLANT RANGE distance and not actual horizontal distance.

notes.front: What advantage does a nondirectional radio beacon have over a VOR?
notes.back: Its low or medium frequencies are not affected by line of sight.
notes.explanation: A VOR, by contrast, is limited by line of sight.
notes.source: Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), ch. 16 “Navigation”, “Automatic Direction Finder (ADF)”, PDF p. 29 (printed 16-29)
notes.evidence: NDBs have one advantage over the VOR in that low or medium frequencies are not affected by line-of-sight. The

notes.front: How many satellites does RAIM need to detect an integrity anomaly?
notes.back: At least 5, or 4 plus barometric altimeter input (baro-aiding).
notes.explanation: RAIM needs one satellite beyond those required for navigation, to check the others.
notes.source: Aeronautical Information Manual, para. 1-1-17 “Global Positioning System (GPS)”
notes.evidence: In order for RAIM to determine if a satellite is providing corrupted information, at least one satellite, in addition to those required for navigation, must be in view for the receiver to perform the RAIM function. RAIM requires a minimum of 5 satellites, or 4 satellites and barometric altimeter input (baro-aiding), to detect an integrity anomaly.

notes.front: What does the first type of RAIM fault message mean?
notes.back: Not enough satellites are available for RAIM; the position may be fine, but its integrity cannot be determined.
notes.explanation: The receiver still navigates, but has lost its ability to check itself.
notes.source: Aeronautical Information Manual, para. 1-1-17 “Global Positioning System (GPS)”
notes.evidence: The first type of message indicates that there are not enough satellites available to provide RAIM integrity monitoring. The GPS navigation solution may be acceptable, but the integrity of the solution cannot be determined.

notes.front: Your hand-held GPS disagrees with your VOR position. What should you suspect, and why?
notes.back: The GPS position: VFR hand-held units have no RAIM alerting, so cross-check it against other navigation.
notes.explanation: Without RAIM the unit cannot warn of a position error, so the manual calls for a systematic cross-check.
notes.source: Aeronautical Information Manual, para. 1-1-17 “Global Positioning System (GPS)”
notes.evidence: RAIM Capability. VFR GPS panel mount receivers and hand-held units have no RAIM alerting capability. This prevents the pilot from being alerted to the loss of the required number of satellites in view, or the detection of a position error. Pilots should use a systematic cross-check with other navigation techniques to verify position.
notes.choices:
A) Suspect the GPS; it has no RAIM alerting
B) Trust the GPS; it is always more accurate
C) Ignore both and continue
notes.choicesExplained: B: without RAIM a VFR unit cannot warn of an error. C: the disagreement is a cue to cross-check, not to ignore.

notes.front: What are the three critical areas of concern when using GPS for VFR?
notes.back: RAIM capability, database currency and antenna location.
notes.explanation: The Aeronautical Information Manual singles out these three for VFR use.
notes.source: Aeronautical Information Manual, para. 1-1-17 “Global Positioning System (GPS)”
notes.evidence: When using GPS for VFR operations, RAIM capability, database currency, and antenna location are critical areas of concern.

notes.front: Must a GPS database be current for VFR navigation?
notes.back: No requirement exists, but databases should be updated, and an outdated one should not drive a moving map near critical airspace.
notes.explanation: The rule differs by operation: IFR use requires a current database, while other use only should have one.
notes.source: Aeronautical Information Manual, para. 1-1-17 “Global Positioning System (GPS)”
notes.evidence: Databases must be updated for IFR operations and should be updated for all other operations. However, there is no requirement for databases to be updated for VFR navigation. It is not recommended to use a moving map with an outdated database in and around critical airspace.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · FAA-S-ACS-6C and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: Your GPS database expired last month and you plan to skirt a Class B area using its moving map. What does the handbook advise?
notes.back: Disregard the moving map for critical navigation decisions; use current charts.
notes.explanation: Pilots have entered airspace they meant to avoid by relying on outdated databases.
notes.source: Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), ch. 16 “Navigation”, “Database Currency”, PDF p. 32 (printed 16-32)
notes.evidence: to VFR pilots wishing to fly around critical airspace areas, such as a Restricted Area or a Class B airspace segment. Numerous pilots have ventured into airspace they were trying to avoid by using an outdated database.
notes.choices:
A) Disregard the map; use current charts
B) Use the map; boundaries rarely change
C) Use the map but fly 500 feet higher
notes.choicesExplained: B: outdated maps have led pilots into airspace they were avoiding. C: an altitude buffer does not fix wrong lateral boundaries.

notes.front: Should a VFR GPS be relied on as the only means of navigation?
notes.back: No: no design standard of accuracy or integrity applies to VFR GPS receivers.
notes.explanation: VFR units should be used alongside other forms of navigation to keep to the planned route.
notes.source: Aeronautical Information Manual, para. 1-1-17 “Global Positioning System (GPS)”
notes.evidence: Do not solely rely on GPS for VFR navigation. No design standard of accuracy or integrity is used for a VFR GPS receiver. VFR GPS receivers should be used in conjunction with other forms of navigation during VFR operations to ensure a correct route of flight is maintained.

notes.front: Besides corrections, how does WAAS improve GPS availability?
notes.back: Its geostationary satellite gives, in effect, an additional GPS satellite in view.
notes.explanation: The same satellite also carries the correction signal.
notes.source: Aeronautical Information Manual, para. 1-1-18 “Wide Area Augmentation System (WAAS)”
notes.evidence: In addition to providing the correction signal, the WAAS GEO provides an additional pseudorange measurement to the aircraft receiver, improving the availability of GPS by providing, in effect, an additional GPS satellite in view.

notes.front: Besides terrain, obstacles and VFR cruising altitudes, what two further factors does the standard list for altitude selection?
notes.back: The airplane’s glide distance and the effect of wind.
notes.explanation: All five appear together in the cross-country planning knowledge element.
notes.source: Private Pilot for Airplane Category ACS (FAA-S-ACS-6C), Area I Task D, Cross-Country Flight Planning, PA.I.D.K2, PDF p. 13
notes.evidence: PA.I.D.K2 Altitude selection accounting for terrain and obstacles, glide distance of airplane, VFR cruising altitudes, and effect of wind.

notes.front: Your engine runs rough and you decide to divert. Should you finish plotting and computing the new course before turning?
notes.back: No: in an emergency, divert promptly toward the alternate, then work out the details.
notes.explanation: Completing all plotting and computation before diverting may only aggravate an actual emergency.
notes.source: Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), ch. 16 “Navigation”, “Flight Diversion”, PDF p. 35 (printed 16-35)
notes.evidence: alternate destination. Attempting to complete all plotting, measuring, and computations involved before diverting to the alternate destination may only aggravate an actual emergency.
notes.choices:
A) No, turn toward the alternate first
B) Yes, accuracy comes first
C) Yes, but only the distance
notes.choicesExplained: B and C: delaying the turn to compute may aggravate the emergency.

notes.front: Once established on the diversion course, what should the pilot work out?
notes.back: Note the time, then use the nearest winds aloft for heading and GS, then a new arrival time and fuel use.
notes.explanation: Only after the turn, with the aircraft established on its new course, does the arithmetic begin.
notes.source: Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), ch. 16 “Navigation”, “Flight Diversion”, PDF p. 35 (printed 16-35)
notes.evidence: Once established on course, note the time, and then use the winds aloft nearest to your diversion point to calculate a heading and GS. Once a GS has been calculated, determine a new arrival time and fuel consumption.

notes.front: Besides cloud heights and winds, what two factors should a diversion altitude account for?
notes.back: Terrain and radio reception.
notes.explanation: The handbook lists all four together for choosing a diversion altitude.
notes.source: Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), ch. 16 “Navigation”, “Flight Diversion”, PDF p. 35 (printed 16-35)
notes.evidence: planning. When determining an altitude to use while diverting, consider cloud heights, winds, terrain, and radio reception.

notes.front: You are unsure of your position and cannot see any town. What does the handbook say to do first?
notes.back: Climb, mindful of traffic and weather.
notes.explanation: Climbing comes before other steps such as radio fixes or calling for help.
notes.source: Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), ch. 16 “Navigation”, “Lost Procedures”, PDF p. 34 (printed 16-34)
notes.evidence: or city cannot be seen, the first thing to do is climb, being
notes.choices:
A) Climb, watching traffic and weather
B) Descend to read road signs
C) Circle until a landmark appears
notes.choicesExplained: B: descending reduces radio and radar coverage. C: circling does not improve reception or fix position.

notes.front: How can a lost pilot with a VOR or ADF find position?
notes.back: By plotting an azimuth from two or more navigation facilities.
notes.explanation: The lines cross at the aircraft’s position.
notes.source: Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), ch. 16 “Navigation”, “Lost Procedures”, PDF p. 34 (printed 16-34)
notes.evidence: an azimuth from two or more navigational facilities. If GPS

notes.front: If being lost becomes threatening, transmit on the emergency frequency {{c1::121.5 MHz}} and set the transponder to 7700.
notes.explanation: It is the step for when being lost turns threatening, not the first resort.
notes.source: Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), ch. 16 “Navigation”, “Lost Procedures”, PDF p. 34 (printed 16-34)
notes.evidence: transmit the situation on the emergency frequency 121.5 MHz

notes.front: Lost and low on fuel, you declare an emergency on 121.5 MHz. What transponder code do you set?
notes.explanation: The handbook pairs the emergency frequency with the 7700 code when the situation becomes threatening.
notes.source: Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), ch. 16 “Navigation”, “Lost Procedures”, PDF p. 34 (printed 16-34)
notes.evidence: and set the transponder to 7700. Most facilities, and even
notes.choicesExplained: B: 1200 is the ordinary VFR code, not an emergency code. C: the handbook names 7700 for this situation.

notes.front: Which two basic radar services for VFR aircraft were once called “Stage I”?
notes.back: Traffic advisories and limited vectoring.
notes.explanation: The term became unnecessary and is no longer used; the services remain part of basic radar service.
notes.source: Aeronautical Information Manual, para. 4-1-18 “Terminal Radar Services for VFR Aircraft”
notes.evidence: When the stage services were developed, two basic radar services (traffic advisories and limited vectoring) were identified as “Stage I.” This definition became unnecessary and the term “Stage I” was eliminated from use.

notes.front: Besides traffic advisories, limited vectoring and sequencing, what basic radar service do all commissioned radar facilities give VFR aircraft?
notes.back: Safety alerts.
notes.explanation: Basic radar service is given by all commissioned radar facilities in addition to controlling IFR aircraft.
notes.source: Aeronautical Information Manual, para. 4-1-18 “Terminal Radar Services for VFR Aircraft”
notes.evidence: In addition to the use of radar for the control of IFR aircraft, all commissioned radar facilities provide the following basic radar services for VFR aircraft: Safety alerts.

notes.front: What does TRSA service provide?
notes.back: Separation between all participating VFR aircraft and all IFR aircraft in the TRSA.
notes.explanation: Pilot participation is urged but not mandatory.
notes.source: Aeronautical Information Manual, para. 4-1-18 “Terminal Radar Services for VFR Aircraft”
notes.evidence: The purpose of this service is to provide separation between all participating VFR aircraft and all IFR aircraft operating within the airspace defined as the Terminal Radar Service Area (TRSA). Pilot participation is urged but is not mandatory.

notes.front: What does Class C service add to basic radar service?
notes.back: Approved separation between IFR and VFR aircraft, and sequencing of VFR arrivals to the primary airport.
notes.explanation: It builds on the basic services every radar facility provides.
notes.source: Aeronautical Information Manual, para. 4-1-18 “Terminal Radar Services for VFR Aircraft”
notes.evidence: This service provides, in addition to basic radar service, approved separation between IFR and VFR aircraft, and sequencing of VFR arrivals to the primary airport.

notes.front: How does Class B radar service differ from Class C service?
notes.back: Class B separates aircraft based on IFR, VFR and/or weight; Class C separates IFR from VFR aircraft.
notes.explanation: Both add separation and sequencing of VFR arrivals to basic radar service.
notes.source: Aeronautical Information Manual, para. 4-1-18 “Terminal Radar Services for VFR Aircraft”
notes.evidence: This service provides, in addition to basic radar service, approved separation of aircraft based on IFR, VFR, and/or weight, and sequencing of VFR arrivals to the primary airport(s).

notes.front: Receiving radar traffic advisories, you are told of no traffic ahead. Are you relieved of looking out?
notes.back: No. Radar services do not relieve the pilot of seeing and avoiding other traffic.
notes.explanation: The manual states the services never replace the pilot’s own vigilance.
notes.source: Aeronautical Information Manual, para. 4-1-15 “Radar Traffic Information Service”
notes.evidence: This service is not intended to relieve the pilot of the responsibility for continual vigilance to see and avoid other aircraft.
notes.choices:
A) No, keep looking out
B) Yes, radar covers all traffic
C) Yes, in Class B only
notes.choicesExplained: B: radar may miss traffic and controllers may be unable to give the service. C: the see-and-avoid duty applies in every class.

notes.front: While receiving VFR radar advisory service, how should the pilot use the radio?
notes.back: Monitor the assigned frequency at all times.
notes.explanation: This spares controllers from worrying about radio failure or an emergency.
notes.source: Aeronautical Information Manual, para. 4-1-15 “Radar Traffic Information Service”
notes.evidence: When receiving VFR radar advisory service, pilots should monitor the assigned frequency at all times. This is to preclude controllers' concern for radio failure or emergency assistance to aircraft under the controller's jurisdiction.

notes.front: Does VFR radar advisory service include vectors away from conflicting traffic?
notes.back: Not unless the pilot requests them.
notes.explanation: Vectors around traffic are available, but only when the pilot asks.
notes.source: Aeronautical Information Manual, para. 4-1-15 “Radar Traffic Information Service”
notes.evidence: VFR radar advisory service does not include vectors away from conflicting traffic unless requested by the pilot.

notes.front: You no longer want flight following and plan to switch to a non-towered airport’s frequency. What should you do?
notes.back: Tell the controller before changing frequency, then set the transponder to 1200 if applicable.
notes.explanation: The order matters: advise the controller first, then change frequency and code.
notes.source: Aeronautical Information Manual, para. 4-1-15 “Radar Traffic Information Service”
notes.evidence: When advisory service is no longer desired, advise the controller before changing frequencies and then change your transponder code to 1200, if applicable.
notes.choices:
A) Tell the controller, then squawk 1200
B) Just change frequency
C) Squawk 7600 and change frequency
notes.choicesExplained: B: silent departure can be treated as a possible emergency. C: 7600 signals radio failure, not the end of the service.

notes.front: Flying north, ATC reports traffic “two o’clock, five miles”. Where do you look?
notes.back: Ahead and to the right, about 60° right of the nose.
notes.explanation: Clock positions are given from your ground track, with 12 o’clock straight ahead; the controller sees only your track, so allow for any wind correction angle.
notes.source: Aeronautical Information Manual, para. 4-1-15 “Radar Traffic Information Service”
notes.evidence: Azimuth from the aircraft in terms of the 12 hour clock, or
notes.choices:
A) Ahead and to the right
B) Behind and to the left
C) North-east of the airport
notes.choicesExplained: B: that would be about eight o’clock. C: the clock position is relative to your aircraft, not the ground.
